source_text: Ratio autem dicti huius in tribus articulis constitit, in re, in tempore, in modo. In re, ut quid sit quaerendum consideres, in tempore, ut quando, in modo, ut quousque. Igitur quaerendum est quod Christus instituit, utique quamdiu non invenis, utique donec invenias. Invenisti autem cum credidisti. Nam non credidisses, si non invenisses, sicut nec quaesisses, nisi ut invenires. Ad hoc ergo quaerens, ut invenias, et ad hoc inveniens, ut credas. Omnem prolationem quaerendi et inveniendi credendo fixisti. Hunc tibi modum statuit fructus ipse quaerendi. Hanc tibi fossam determinavit ipse qui te non vult aliud credere quam quod instituit, ideoque nec quaerere. Ceterum si quia et alia tanta ab aliis sunt instituta, propterea in tantum quaerere debemus in quantum possumus invenire, semper quaerimus et nunquam omnino credimus. Ubi enim erit finis quaerendi? ubi statio credendi? ubi expunctio inveniendi? Apud Marcionem? Sed et Valentinus proponit, Quaerite et invenietis. Apud Valentinum? Sed et Apelles hac me pronuntiatione pulsabit, et Hebion et Simon et omnes ex ordine non habent aliud quo se mihi insinuantes me sibi addicant. Ero itaque nusquam, dum ubique convenio, Quaerite et invenietis, et velut si nusquam; quasi qui nunquam apprehenderim illud quod Christus instituit, quod quaeri oportet, quod credi necesse est.
thought_title: The limits of seeking: what, when, and how far
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that the command 'Seek and you will find' has fixed limits, and that once a person has believed what Christ instituted, seeking must stop.
pass_a_gloss: But the reason of this saying consists in three points: in the thing, in the time, in the manner. In the thing, that you consider what is to be sought; in the time, when; in the manner, how far. Therefore what Christ instituted is to be sought, certainly as long as you do not find, certainly until you find. But you have found when you have believed. For you would not have believed, if you had not found, just as you would not have sought, except in order that you might find. Therefore seeking in order that you may find, and finding in order that you may believe. By believing you have fixed every extension of seeking and finding. The very fruit of seeking has established this limit for you. He himself has determined this boundary for you, who does not want you to believe anything other than what he instituted, and therefore not to seek either. But if because many other things also have been instituted by others, for that reason we ought to seek as far as we are able to find, we always seek and never at all believe. For where will be the end of seeking? where the stopping-point of believing? where the completion of finding? With Marcion? But Valentinus also proposes, 'Seek and you will find.' With Valentinus? But Apelles also will knock at me with this pronouncement, and Ebion and Simon and all in order have nothing else by which, insinuating themselves to me, they may bind me to themselves. Therefore I shall be nowhere, while everywhere I meet, 'Seek and you will find,' and as if nowhere; as one who has never grasped that which Christ instituted, which ought to be sought, which must be believed.

choices.why: Prolatio means a bringing forward or extension; here it denotes the prolonging or drawing out of the process of seeking and finding, which belief brings to an end.
Fossa literally means a ditch or trench, used here metaphorically for a fixed limit or boundary line that Christ has dug to mark off what is to be believed.
Statio means a standing-place or halt; paired with finis and expunctio, it conveys the fixed point where believing comes to rest.
Expunctio means a marking off or finishing; it renders the idea of finding being brought to its final point.
Pulsare means to strike or knock; here it conveys Apelles pressing Tertullian with the same pronouncement, as if knocking at his door with an argument.
Addicere in legal language means to adjudge or assign someone to another; here it conveys the heretics claiming Tertullian as their own adherent.

pass_b_english: The reasoning behind this saying rests on three points: the thing, the time, and the manner. The thing, so that you consider what is to be sought; the time, when; the manner, how far. What is to be sought, then, is what Christ instituted—as long, of course, as you have not found it, and until you do find it. You have found it when you have believed. For you would not have believed if you had not found it, just as you would not have sought unless you intended to find. So you sought in order to find, and you found in order to believe. By believing, you have brought the whole extension of seeking and finding to a fixed end. The very fruit of seeking has set this limit for you. The one who does not want you to believe anything other than what he instituted—and therefore does not want you to seek anything else—has dug this boundary for you. Otherwise, if because so many other things have been instituted by others we must keep seeking as long as we can keep finding, then we will always be seeking and never actually believe. Where will the end of seeking be? Where the stopping-point of believing? Where the completion of finding? With Marcion? But Valentinus also proposes, “Seek and you will find” (Matthew 7:7). With Valentinus? But Apelles will knock at me with this pronouncement too, and Ebion and Simon and all the rest in turn have nothing else by which they insinuate themselves to me and bind me to themselves. So I will be nowhere, while everywhere I am met with “Seek and you will find”—and as if I were nowhere, as if I had never grasped what Christ instituted, what ought to be sought, what must be believed.
